title: Calorie‐Free Menus as a Potential Mitigation Strategy for Mandatory Calorie Labelling: Evidence From People With Disordered Eating in England
abstract: ABSTRACT Objective Since the introduction of mandatory out‐of‐home calorie labelling in England, concerns have been raised about potential negative impacts on people with disordered eating. To mitigate these concerns, food outlets can provide calorie‐free menus on request. However, no research has explored their use or impact among people with disordered eating. Method We conducted a cross‐sectional mixed methods study on the wider impacts of calorie labelling among 1001 people aged ≥ 16 years in England with lived experience of disordered eating. Of these, 969 completed questions about calorie‐free menus. In‐depth quantitative analyses focused on 644 participants who reported negative impact of calorie labels (i.e., those who may benefit from calorie‐free menus). Results Most people did not request calorie‐free menus (63.88%), including those that reported negative impacts (53.57%). People with higher clinical impairment, current compensatory behaviours, current comorbid disorder, and a history of eating disorder treatment were more likely to use calorie‐free menus. Qualitative analyses highlighted both practical barriers and social discomfort when accessing calorie‐free menus. Those who did use calorie‐free menus reported positive experiences. Conclusions People with disordered eating may benefit from accessing calorie‐free menus. Addressing practical and social barriers may improve eating experiences of people with disordered eating in the out‐of‐home sector.
